items.title: Why a deadline makes your stomach knot
items.text:
Why a deadline makes your stomach knot

You feel a knot in your stomach whenever a deadline looms, but ancient hunters and modern scientists say that knot is a relic of a different fight.

Evidence: Hans Selye (1936, Canada): Chronic pressure spikes cortisol by about 15 to 20 percent; Michael Gurven et al. (2015, Tanzania): Hadza average cortisol about 30 percent lower than industrial societies

MindLore: how your mind works, from real research.

items.title: Pain of Isolation
items.text:
Pain of Isolation

You feel physical pain when your friends leave you out.

Evidence: Naomi Eisenberger (2003, University of California, Los Angeles): Social rejection activates the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, the same region that processes physical pain.; Matthew Lieberman and Naomi Eisenberger (2004, UCLA): The social attachment system evolved in early mammals to hijack physical pain pathways to prevent separation.

items.title: Why Silence Heals Your Brain
items.text:

You live in a world of constant background noise.

Evidence: Luciano Bernardi (2006, University of Pavia): Two minutes of silence after listening to music caused a greater decrease in heart rate and blood pressure than the music itself; Mathias Basner (2014, University of Pennsylvania): Noise exposure leads to chronic activation of the sympathetic nervous system and elevated stress hormones like cortisol

items.title: Your Joy Is Wild
items.text:
Your Joy Is Wild

You think play is just silly entertainment.

Evidence: Jaak Panksepp (1990s, Bowling Green State University): Rats emit 50-kHz ultrasonic vocalizations (laughter) during rough-and-tumble play mediated by a subcortical play system.; Marc Bekoff (2004, University of Colorado): Wild canines use specific play bows as an honest communicative signal to negotiate social play and avoid real fighting.

items.title: Your Eyes Blink During Story Turns
items.text:
Your Eyes Blink During Story Turns

You blink your eyes right when a story takes an unexpected turn.

Evidence: Tamami Nakano (2012, Osaka University): People automatically blink at narrative breaks and video scene cuts to reset brain attention networks.; Cognitive Neuroscience Researchers (2010s, Japan): Blinking operates as a cognitive reset button during auditory and visual story transitions in both adults and children.

items.title: Your Face Freezes On Sudden News
items.text:
Your Face Freezes On Sudden News

You widen your eyes when hearing unexpected news.

Evidence: Adam Anderson (2014, Cornell University): Widening eyes increases visual field and eye movement speed to detect visual information.; Adam Anderson (2017, Cornell University): Gasping and facial expressions linked to fear increase nasal capacity and air intake.

items.title: Your Sudden Laughter Reveals Ancient Survival
items.text:
Your Sudden Laughter Reveals Ancient Survival

You laugh out loud when someone tickles your ribs.

Evidence: Jaak Panksepp (2000, Bowling Green State University): Rats emit 50 kilohertz ultrasonic chirps that function as laughter during play and tickling; Comparative neuroscientists and biologists (2000s, Worldwide research labs): Play vocalizations like panting and chirping serve as non-aggressive play signals across multiple mammal species
